# SamoFlow — PROJECT_SPEC (living context — read at the start of every session, update after every task)

## 1. What we are building and why

A production-ready, multi-tenant, embeddable AI widget platform: one website is one tenant, with its own site key(s) and its own `client_id` in Qdrant. The widget answers visitors only from that tenant's own content (crawled pages, listed URLs, uploaded files, synced database data), streams answers in real time, remembers a returning visitor's earlier chats in the same browser, and hands off to a human through an escalation request when the AI cannot help. Full detail: docs/SPEC.md.

## 2. How to work (rules for every session)

1. At the start of a session, read this file and tell me the current task, the next task and any open markers. Do not write code until I say so.
2. One task at a time. Implement only what I name. Do not modify completed tasks.
3. When starting a component, create a skeleton first: stubs that raise NotImplementedError with a TODO(<task-id>) comment explaining what each does, its inputs and its outputs.
4. Keep code simple with short comments. After writing code, add inline markers: ASSUMPTION (something I should verify), UNCERTAIN (something you are unsure about), TODO(<task-id>) (something incomplete). If similar logic already exists, add a NOTE pointing to it instead of duplicating it.
5. Write tests with the code, covering normal cases, edge cases, expected failures and bad inputs (empty, None, wrong type, oversized). Run them and show the real output. Never weaken, skip or delete a test to get green.
6. Finish each task with a report: what changed, test results, deviations from the spec, open questions. Then update this file and stop. Do not start the next task.
7. If the spec is ambiguous, or you want to deviate from it, stop and ask. Record approved deviations under Decisions made.
8. Ask before adding any dependency (name, purpose, alternatives considered).
9. Run a duplication check after every 3rd task, and never go past 4 tasks without one.
10. Clean code means resolved markers: verify then remove ASSUMPTION, resolve then remove UNCERTAIN, finish then remove TODO. A phase is not accepted while any ASSUMPTION or UNCERTAIN marker remains, and every remaining TODO must be listed under Open markers with the task that owns it.
11. Follow widely adopted industry practice and library defaults, including standard security measures: validate input at trust boundaries, use least privilege and secure defaults, keep secrets and sensitive data out of code, logs and error messages, keep dependencies current, and use well-known framework or library mechanisms instead of custom security schemes. Do not add abstractions, options, checks or tests the task does not need. When the choice is between a standard default and a custom rule, use the default unless the spec says otherwise. Security requirements in the spec and in the engineering rules are never optional and always win over simplicity. If you are unsure whether something is needed for security, or you think something is over-engineered, too rigid or insecure, say so and ask me before building it.

## 3. Engineering rules and commands

- Commands: make up, make test, make lint, make migrate, make evals, make hooks (lists TODO, ASSUMPTION, UNCERTAIN and NOTE markers in the code).
- Tenant identity comes only from the verified token. Never accept client_id, visitor id, thread_id or checkpoint ids from the client. Verify conversation_id by database lookup.
- All Qdrant reads go through retrieve(), and the client_id filter is applied inside every sub-query.
- All tenant-scoped database access goes through the tenant-scoped repository helpers.
- The model never writes contact details and has no tool with side effects. Escalation is submitted by the visitor's browser.
- Everything is async. No blocking calls in handlers. Never hold a DB connection while streaming.
- Migrations via Alembic only. Secrets never in the repository.
- Treat all ingested text, tool output and visitor messages as untrusted input.
- Nothing hard-coded that should be configuration (limits, thresholds, paths, URLs).
- Any deviation from the spec is recorded in the decisions log (see SPEC section 3) in the same change.
- After each phase, run the acceptance checks and summarize deviations before starting the next.
- Convention (written down at the duplication check after 2.4.b/c/d, previously applied ad hoc): when a task adds a new test file, run it standalone and re-run it 3 times before trusting the result, to catch any ordering-dependent or flaky behavior a single pass wouldn't surface.
- Convention (written down at the duplication check after 2.5.d/e/f): every decision-log entry, including a duplication check's own consolidated entry, ends with its own `Verified:` paragraph stating the real commands run and their real output — never only a prose summary of what changed. A duplication check's final verification pass happens after all accepted fixes are applied, as a separate step from each fix's own small per-fix check; write that final pass into its own `Verified:` paragraph before closing the entry, not folded into the summary bullet alone.
- Convention (written down at the duplication check after 3.2.b/c/d): every decision that defers work to another step or phase is written as a real §9 Open marker, with its owner, in the same edit that records the decision — never left as decision-log prose alone to be promoted later.
- 2026-11-03: a standing "Senior engineer judgment" rule is now recorded in CLAUDE.md (not copied here — a project-independent rule, not a SamoFlow spec decision) — extends rule 11 and rule 6 above; applies to every task.
- Convention (written down at the Task 3.5.e duplication check, 2026-10-13): every manual/research script under backend/scripts/ that writes to Qdrant uses its own disposable collection name, or deletes every point it seeded (by tenant_id) in a try/finally — confirmed live, all 7 existing scripts already comply; this just makes the convention explicit so a future one doesn't skip it.

## 5. Decisions made

- 2026-09-19: Shadow DOM isolates the widget from the host page (SPEC §11).
- 2026-09-19: One website = one tenant, with its own site key(s) and `client_id` (SPEC §4.1).
- 2026-09-19: Visitors are recognized by browser now; logged-in users (`external_user_id`) are a later phase (SPEC §4.1, §19).
- 2026-09-19: A visitor can have several conversations, shown as a "previous chats" list (SPEC §4.5).
- 2026-09-19: Chat retention is per-tenant, default 30 days, allowed range 1–90 days (SPEC §4.6).
- 2026-09-19: Content sources: URL list, crawl, uploads, database sync, any combination (SPEC §5.1).
- 2026-09-19: All sources are answerable to any visitor; a warning is shown when uploads/DB content is added; one-click disable/delete per source (SPEC §5).
- 2026-09-19: Domain ownership is verified once (file, meta tag or DNS), never re-checked; the platform admin can revoke or force re-verification. Revocation stops fetching only — already-indexed content stays answerable until the source is disabled/deleted or the site is suspended (SPEC §5.5).
- 2026-09-19: English only for v1 (SPEC §3).
- 2026-09-19: Refresh cadence is daily/weekly/monthly/quarterly plus refresh-now, gated by plan (SPEC §5.4).
- 2026-09-19: Plan limits live in a `limits` JSON, assigned manually; payments come later (SPEC §5.4).
- 2026-09-19: Crawler is simple (no JS rendering) for v1 (SPEC §5.5, §19).
- 2026-09-19: Upload types: PDF, .docx, .txt/.md (SPEC §5.6).
- 2026-09-19: Database sync is scheduled first; approved live queries are a later phase (SPEC §5.6, §19).
- 2026-09-19: Supported database engines: MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL first (SPEC §5.6).
- 2026-09-19: Hybrid search (dense + sparse BM25, server-side RRF); reranker hook off by default (SPEC §6.3).
- 2026-09-19: Follow-up questions are rewritten by a small fast model; original message used on rewrite failure/timeout (SPEC §6.3).
- 2026-09-19: Three specialists (Retrieval, Fallback & Guardrail, Escalation Coordinator), rule-based routing, no LLM hop (SPEC §6.1–6.2).
- 2026-09-19: The AI has no tools with side effects; escalation is submitted by the visitor's browser (SPEC §8).
- 2026-09-19: We build and run tools first; tenant tool servers are a later phase (SPEC §8, §19).
- 2026-09-19: Unanswerable questions get a fixed fallback with the tenant's support details, never a guess (SPEC §6.3).
- 2026-09-19: Citations are shown for web pages only; no labels for uploads or database content (SPEC §6.3).
- 2026-09-19: Human handoff is an escalation request (email + dashboard inbox), retained 12 months by default, allowed range 1–24 months (SPEC §7).
- 2026-09-19: Monthly quota counts AI-answered messages only; tenant alerted at 80% and 100% (SPEC §9).
- 2026-09-19: Abuse defense is rate limits only for v1; a challenge (e.g. Turnstile) is deferred (SPEC §9, §19).
- 2026-09-19: A dropped connection cancels the run with no partial answer saved; retry reuses the same `client_message_id` (SPEC §10).
- 2026-09-19: Dashboard login is email/password, with an owner who can invite team members (SPEC §12).
- 2026-09-19: Widget customization is limited to colors, logo, title, greeting and position; no custom CSS in v1 (SPEC §11).
- 2026-09-19: Hosting is one Ubuntu server with Docker Compose for v1 (SPEC §14, §19).
- 2026-09-19: Phoenix trace text is stored 30 days then auto-deleted, with a per-tenant opt-out (SPEC §13).
- 2026-09-19: Plan page cap counts total indexed web pages only (crawl + URL-list); uploads are capped by storage/size and database sync by row count (SPEC §5.4, §5.5).
- 2026-09-19: Supported database engines confirmed as MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL (SPEC §5.6).
- 2026-09-19: The relevance threshold is a platform default; only the platform admin can override it per tenant, and it is not tenant-editable (SPEC §6.3).
- 2026-09-19: Email is sent through our own SMTP server, behind a provider-neutral interface (SPEC §14).
- 2026-09-19: Escalation trigger phrases live in a YAML file in the repo (roughly 50–200 entries, each with a category and a golden-set test reference), schema-validated in CI; every change goes through a deploy and the golden-set tests (SPEC §7).
- 2026-09-19: A site key moves from `draft` to `live` only through a server-side check (at least one contact method and one allowed origin); draft keys work from allowed origins with a test-mode badge (SPEC §4.1, §6.3).

- 2026-09-20: Step 1.1.f — `backend/app/worker.py`'s `run(stop)` calls `get_settings()` only, logs one INFO line containing `app_env` only (never database_url/qdrant_url), then awaits the stop event; `main()` configures logging, registers SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers via `loop.add_signal_handler` that set the stop event, and exits 0 on clean shutdown or non-zero with no traceback on `SettingsError`. No job logic, no polling loop, no dependency on Postgres/Qdrant. Verified by hand: with the signal-handler registration removed, `SIGTERM`'s default OS disposition still terminates the (unhandled) process quickly rather than hanging it — the process exits with code -15 (terminated by signal), not 0, so the test still fails fast on `assert exit_code == 0` rather than by hitting the 10-second `wait_for` timeout.

- 2026-09-20: Step 1.1.h — Alembic skeleton generated with `alembic init` (default generic template, alembic==1.20.0) then trimmed: `alembic.ini` keeps `script_location = %(here)s/alembic` (the tool's own default), drops the noise comments and the unused `sqlalchemy.url` placeholder line (no database URL lives in the ini); the generated `README` is deleted; `alembic/versions/.gitkeep` keeps the empty directory in git (git does not track empty folders, and Alembic fails if the folder is missing). `alembic/env.py` gets its URL from `get_settings().database_url_str()` and builds the engine directly with `sqlalchemy.create_engine(url, poolclass=NullPool)`; it never calls `config.set_main_option` — verified by hand that pattern breaks with `ValueError: invalid interpolation syntax` on a literal "%" in the password, and would also copy the secret into the Config object. Offline mode is dropped (not "enough extra code to be free"): supporting it without `set_main_option` would need its own URL-plumbing, so only online mode exists; `target_metadata = None` with a `TODO(1.2)` marker (models arrive in 1.2). `backend/tests/test_config_guard.py` (Task 1.1.c's guard) now also scans `backend/alembic` and allow-lists `alembic/env.py` in `ALLOWED_DATABASE_URL_CALLERS` — verified by hand that a scratch file elsewhere calling `database_url_str()` still fails the guard.
- 2026-09-20: Step 1.1.h — Test database is Option A: integration tests read `TEST_DATABASE_URL` from the environment (never construct one from parts). `require_test_database()` (backend/tests/conftest.py) is the single guarded entry point: unset + `CI` != "true" → `pytest.skip` with the local `docker run` command; unset + `CI` == "true" → `pytest.fail` (CI must run this test, not silently skip it); set but not a `postgresql+psycopg` URL naming a database ending in `_test` → `pytest.fail`, never skip, and before anything is touched — this is the safety rail that keeps the test's `DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE` off a real database. `backend/tests/test_alembic.py`'s integration test resets the schema through a sync SQLAlchemy engine, then runs `python -m alembic upgrade head` as a subprocess (harness env: `APP_ENV=test`, `QDRANT_URL`/`API_HOST`/`API_PORT` harmless, `DATABASE_URL` = the test URL) twice, asserting exit 0 both times, that the public schema then contains exactly `alembic_version` (Alembic does create it with zero revisions), and that neither run's captured stdout/stderr contains the real password.
- 2026-09-20: Step 1.1.h — Postgres tag for the local/CI test database: `postgres:18.2-trixie`, verified to exist with `docker manifest inspect` (18.2 is the newest patch of the newest stable major, 18, published for Debian trixie as of 2026-09-20; 19.0 and 18.3 do not exist yet).
- 2026-09-20: Step 1.1.h — `backend/Dockerfile`'s final stage now also copies `alembic.ini` (`COPY --chmod=0644`) and `alembic/` (`COPY --chmod=0755`, so the directory stays traversable) alongside the existing `entrypoint.sh` copy — root-owned, not writable by the app user (verified by hand: `touch` as uid 10001 fails with Permission denied on both). `entrypoint.sh` gained a third mode, `migrate`, that runs `exec alembic upgrade head`; it does not check `API_HOST`/`API_PORT` itself, since `migrate` never uses them and `get_settings()` still validates all five required variables when `alembic/env.py` calls it. Usage message updated to `{api|worker|migrate}`.

No per-file-ignore was needed in `pyproject.toml`, and the template `env.py` (once rewritten per the design above) passes lint with no ignores at all.

Accepted as a residual risk for now because: hatchling is already pinned to an exact version in `[build-system] requires` (not a floating range); the runtime image ships no build tools or pip at all once 1.1.o.d lands, so a compromised build backend cannot act again after the image is built, only during it; and CI has no secrets for a malicious build step to exfiltrate.

Traced `actions/runner`'s `NodeScriptActionHandler.cs` (the code that launches a JS action like this one): absent an override, it launches with `workingDirectory = GetGitHubContext("workspace")`, i.e. `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE` — which is also where `actions/checkout` places the repo by default. On paper, this chain should have found `.grype.yaml` at the repo root. It plainly didn't in the real run, and the local Docker-based checks done for the first follow-up entry (mounting the repo as the container's cwd) couldn't have caught the gap, because they only ever exercised the CWD-based auto-detection path working correctly — they never tested the failure mode itself. Added a matching regression check to `backend/tests/test_ci_guard.py`'s `_security_specific_violations`: the `anchore/scan-action` step's block must contain the literal `config: ${{ github.workspace }}/.grype.yaml` string, not just any `config:` line. - 2026-09-26: Step 1.2.a — async DB engine/session plumbing (`backend/app/db.py`). Driver-scheme finding, verified against the installed `sqlalchemy==2.0.54`/`psycopg==3.3.6` (not assumed): `DATABASE_URL`'s existing `postgresql+psycopg` scheme (psycopg 3, sync-driver form) needs **no change** for `create_async_engine()`. Confirmed by hand: psycopg 3 (unlike psycopg2) natively supports both sync and async connections through the one driver package; SQLAlchemy's psycopg dialect module exposes a `PGDialect_psycopg.get_async_dialect_cls()` classmethod for exactly this, and constructing `create_async_engine("postgresql+psycopg://...")` resolves to `PGDialectAsync_psycopg` (`engine.dialect.is_async is True`, `engine.dialect.driver == "psycopg"`) with no real connection attempted. `get_engine()`/`_session_factory()` are `@lru_cache`-wrapped (same lazy-singleton pattern as `get_settings()` itself) rather than built at raw module level: a literal top-level `create_async_engine(get_settings()...)` would call `get_settings()` at import time and violate the project's existing zero-import-side-effects convention (`get_settings()` raises `SettingsError` on an invalid/empty environment) — confirmed `create_async_engine()` itself is lazy (no connection until first checkout), but `get_settings()` is not, so the laziness has to be applied at the `get_engine()` level, not assumed to come free from SQLAlchemy alone. `get_db_session()` is a plain async-generator "dependency with yield" function (FastAPI's own documented pattern for DB sessions), not `@asynccontextmanager`-wrapped, so it plugs into `Depends()` unchanged later; non-FastAPI callers (e.g. 1.2.d's repository) drive it with `contextlib.aclosing()`. Pool size left at SQLAlchemy's defaults per the 1.2-breakdown decision (Phase 7 tunes it). One deviation from the task's stated file list, necessary and applied: `backend/tests/test_config_guard.py`'s `ALLOWED_DATABASE_URL_CALLERS` gained `"app/db.py"` (one line) — the pre-existing guard test would otherwise fail, since `db.py` is the second file (after `alembic/env.py`) allowed to call `database_url_str()`. Test design note: `db.py`'s `@lru_cache` engine is a correct process-lifetime singleton for the real app (one event loop for the process), but pytest-asyncio's default function-scoped event loop means each test gets a new loop, so `backend/tests/test_db.py`'s `_fresh_engine` fixture clears the cache and disposes the engine per test — test-harness plumbing only, confirmed via pytest-asyncio's own source (`asyncio_default_test_loop_scope` defaults to `"function"`, unchanged by this project's `pyproject.toml`). New open marker added (§9): nothing calls `get_engine().dispose()` at shutdown yet, since no app lifecycle hook exists until a real consumer wires one up. Two factual claims verified for real against the pinned `postgres:18.2-trixie` image (not assumed), both confirmed true: (1) `gen_random_uuid()` works with **zero extensions installed** (`pg_extension` showed only `plpgsql`) — moved into Postgres core in PG13+, so every UUID PK uses `server_default=text("gen_random_uuid()")`, generated at the DB layer regardless of which process writes a row; (2) Postgres does **not** auto-index foreign-key columns (unlike MySQL/InnoDB) — a live `CREATE TABLE ... REFERENCES` test showed only the referenced table's own PK index existed, nothing on the FK column — confirming every `tenant_id` (and `site_keys.key`) needed an explicit `index=True`, which all five tables now have. `status` columns use plain `String`, not a native Postgres `ENUM` type, for migration flexibility (adding an enum value needs `ALTER TYPE`, more operationally awkward than a plain string); `site_keys.status` gets an explicit `CheckConstraint` restricting it to `draft`/`live`/`suspended` since docs/SPEC.md §4.1 names that exact closed set, but `tenants.status` gets no constraint since no vocabulary is given anywhere in the spec (flagged as an ASSUMPTION in the model and as a new open marker, owner not yet scheduled). `tenants.plan_id` is nullable (§5.4: "plans are assigned manually," implying a tenant can exist before one is assigned). `plans.id` is a UUID (not a fixed string/enum id) for consistency with every other table's PK style, rather than a second PK scheme for one table (rule 11). - 2026-09-27: Step 1.2.d — tenant-scoped repository core (`backend/app/tenancy/repository.py`, `TenantScopedRepository`). Immutability mechanism: `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, the standard-library mechanism (rule 11 — a well-known mechanism over a hand-rolled `__setattr__` override); any post-`__init__` attribute assignment raises `dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError` (confirmed by hand to be a subclass of `AttributeError`), verified directly rather than assumed. Fields are named plainly (`tenant_id`, `session`, no leading underscore): the enforcement comes from `frozen=True` itself, not from hiding the name, and a plain name keeps the constructor call (`TenantScopedRepository(tenant_id=..., session=...)`) idiomatic. `tenant_id` has no default (omitting it raises Python's own `TypeError`); `__post_init__` additionally rejects an explicit `tenant_id=None` (`ValueError`), since a required field only guarantees the argument was passed, not that it's a real value. Two concrete methods prove the pattern: `get_conversation_by_id(cid)` and `list_site_keys()`, both filtering on `self.tenant_id` unconditionally — no method anywhere on the class accepts a `tenant_id` parameter. One necessary deviation from the task's stated file list, flagged before building: `backend/tests/test_app_skeleton.py`'s `STUB_ENTRY_POINTS` had to drop its `("app.tenancy.repository", "get_tenant_scoped_repository")` entry, since that stub function no longer exists / no longer raises `NotImplementedError` once real functionality replaced it — same kind of pre-existing-guard-test fix as 1.2.a's `ALLOWED_DATABASE_URL_CALLERS` edit. Real bug caught by running the new test file standalone rather than trusting the full-suite run: `backend/tests/test_tenancy_repository.py` initially passed only inside `make test-all` by accident, because `test_models.py`/`test_alembic.py` (imported earlier in the same pytest session) had already registered `app.plans.models`'s `plans` table onto the shared `Base.metadata` — the new file never imported `app.plans.models` itself, so `Base.metadata.create_all()` failed with `NoReferencedTableError` on `tenants.plan_id` when run in isolation. Fixed by adding the same side-effect import (`from app.plans import models as plans_models  # noqa: F401`) already used in `alembic/env.py` and `test_models.py`. Security proof, against the real test database (two tenants, one site_key and one conversation each): `list_site_keys()` scoped to tenant A returns only tenant A's site key; `get_conversation_by_id(tenant_B_cid)` — a real, valid row belonging to the wrong tenant — returns `None`, not tenant B's conversation; `get_conversation_by_id(tenant_A_cid)` correctly returns tenant A's own conversation, proving the mechanism isn't just blocking everything. Verified: `make lint` clean; full `backend/tests` without a test database: **133 passed, 8 skipped** (up from 130 passed, 5 skipped — 3 new structural tests run for real, 3 new security-proof tests skip as expected); `make test-all` against the real test-db: **141 passed** (133 + the 8 previously-skipped, all for real, re-run clean after the metadata-import fix); `git status --short` showed exactly the expected files (`backend/app/tenancy/repository.py` modified, `backend/tests/test_tenancy_repository.py` new, plus the flagged `test_app_skeleton.py` fix). `tenancy/repository.py`'s `TODO(1.2)` marker resolved and its open-markers line removed.

- 2026-09-27: Step 1.2.e — CRUD/lookup functions on `TenantScopedRepository`, plus `create_tenant()`. Tenant-creation location: `create_tenant(session, name, status) -> Tenant`, a plain module-level function in `backend/app/tenancy/repository.py`, deliberately never a method on `TenantScopedRepository` — a brand-new tenant has no `tenant_id` yet to scope by, which the class's own constructor invariant (always requires a real `tenant_id`) cannot represent, so a separate function makes "this is the one unscoped operation" structurally visible rather than a special-cased method fighting the class's own guarantee. site_key_id/vid verification: `create_visitor(site_key_id, secret_hash)` and `create_conversation(vid, title=None)` both verify the given foreign id belongs to `self.tenant_id` before creating the row (raising `ValueError` otherwise), rather than trusting the FK constraints already on those columns (`visitors.site_key_id -> site_keys.id`, `conversations.vid -> visitors.vid`) to be enough — a foreign key only proves the referenced row *exists*, not that it belongs to the same tenant, and nothing else in the codebase yet guarantees that (1.4's session endpoint, the only other place that would touch this, doesn't exist yet), so skipping the check would silently accept a tenant-A visitor pointing at tenant B's site_key, or a tenant-A conversation pointing at tenant B's visitor. `get_tenant()` returns the repository's own bound tenant via `scalar_one()` (not `_or_none()`), since a `TenantScopedRepository` is only ever constructed with a real tenant's id — a missing row there is a real error, not a normal "not found." `create_site_key()` always creates in `"draft"` status (docs/SPEC.md §4.1/§6.3: a key moves to `live` only through a separate server-side check, not this method's job). Security proof, against the real test database (same two-tenant fixture as 1.2.d, extended with a visitor per tenant): `get_tenant()` scoped to A returns only A; `create_site_key`/`create_visitor`/`create_conversation` all set `tenant_id` automatically from `self.tenant_id`; `create_visitor` given tenant B's real `site_key_id` and `create_conversation` given tenant B's real `vid` both raise `ValueError`, not silently succeed; `get_visitor_by_id` mirrors `get_conversation_by_id`'s hostile-caller/own-row pair; `create_tenant()` proved to create a real, independently-verifiable row with no tenant scoping involved, and confirmed absent from `TenantScopedRepository` via `hasattr`. Caught by running the extended test file standalone before trusting the full-suite run (same lesson as 1.2.d): none this time — the existing `plans` side-effect import was already in place from 1.2.d's fix, so the new tests passed standalone on the first try. Verified: `make lint` clean; full `backend/tests` without a test database: **134 passed, 17 skipped** (up from 133 passed, 8 skipped — 1 new structural test runs for real, 9 new security-proof tests skip as expected); `make test-all` against the real test-db: **151 passed** (134 + the 17 previously-skipped, all for real); `git status --short` showed exactly the two expected files.

- 2026-09-28: Step 1.3.c — Collection schema, in `app/qdrant.py`. Module constants (not `Settings` fields, rule 11 — nothing else needs them configurable yet): `COLLECTION_NAME = "knowledge_chunks"`, `DENSE_VECTOR_NAME = "dense"`, `SPARSE_VECTOR_NAME = "sparse"`, `DENSE_VECTOR_SIZE = 1536` (`ASSUMPTION`: `text-embedding-3-small`'s output dimension — see the new open marker below, owned by Step 2.5), `CLIENT_ID_FIELD = "client_id"`, `SOURCE_ID_FIELD = "source_id"`. Distance is `Distance.COSINE` (`qdrant_client.http.models`), matching docs/SPEC.md §5.2 and `text-embedding-3-small`'s own intended similarity metric. §5.2's fuller payload field list (`source_type`, `doc_id`, `title`, etc.) is documented there but deliberately not indexed here — only `client_id` and `source_id` get a payload index at this step, per the approved design ("no other payload indexes"); the rest arrive with ingestion (2.4/2.5) if/when a query needs to filter on them.

  Repair-versus-fail rule: `ensure_collection(client, name=COLLECTION_NAME)` creates the collection and both indexes if the collection does not exist; if it exists, it fetches the real config and diffs it against the expected schema. A payload index that is entirely *absent* is repaired (created — additive, covers a crash between `create_collection` and index creation); every other difference (wrong dense size, wrong distance, a missing vector, a sparse vector without the IDF modifier, an index present with the wrong parameters, e.g. `client_id` without `is_tenant`) raises `CollectionSchemaMismatch` naming every difference, never silently replaced. A 409 from `create_collection` (two callers racing) is caught narrowly by status code and falls through to the same verify-then-repair-or-raise path, rather than being swallowed or treated as any other error.

  The comparison lives in a pure function, `_schema_differences(actual_collection_info, name) -> list[str]` (composing four small per-aspect helpers, `_dense_vector_diff`/`_sparse_vector_diff`/`_client_id_index_diff`/`_source_id_index_diff`, plus `_mismatch_message(diffs, name) -> str` for the exception text) — no IO, unit-tested offline with hand-built `qdrant_client.http.models.CollectionInfo` objects (`backend/tests/test_qdrant_collection.py`).

  Exact API surface and field paths, verified live against qdrant-client==1.19.1 and the pinned qdrant/qdrant:v1.19.1 server (test-qdrant), not assumed from memory: `AsyncQdrantClient.create_collection(vectors_config={name: VectorParams(size, distance)}, sparse_vectors_config={name: SparseVectorParams(modifier=Modifier.IDF)})`; `create_payload_index(field_schema=KeywordIndexParams(type=PayloadSchemaType.KEYWORD, is_tenant=True))` for client_id, `field_schema=PayloadSchemaType.KEYWORD` (bare) for source_id. Read back via `get_collection()` → `CollectionInfo`: `.config.params.vectors` is `dict[str, VectorParams]` (`.size`, `.distance`); `.config.params.sparse_vectors` is `dict[str, SparseVectorParams]` (`.modifier`, an enum, `None` when no modifier was set); `.payload_schema` is `dict[str, PayloadIndexInfo]` (`.data_type`, a `PayloadSchemaType` enum; `.params` is `None` unless the index was created with explicit `KeywordIndexParams`, in which case `.params.is_tenant` is the real boolean — `False` if explicitly set that way, `None`/absent-`params` if never set). A duplicate `create_collection` call on an existing name raises `qdrant_client.http.exceptions.UnexpectedResponse` with `status_code == 409`, confirmed live.

  HNSW finding (Qdrant's own docs, fetched directly, not recalled from memory): multitenancy guidance recommends `hnsw_config.m = 0` (disables the global HNSW index) together with `hnsw_config.payload_m` (a non-zero per-tenant value, e.g. 16) alongside `is_tenant=True` on the tenant payload index, so Qdrant builds one HNSW index per tenant group instead of one global index — meaningfully faster for large multi-tenant collections. Separately confirmed: `hnsw_config` (including `m`/`payload_m`) can be changed on an *existing* collection via the update-collection-parameters API without recreating it (supported since Qdrant 1.4) — the server rebuilds affected segments in the background to match. Not built now (out of this task's approved design); see the new open marker below.

- 2026-09-28: Step 1.3.d — Isolation proof at the filter/index level, in `app/qdrant.py` (`tenant_filter()`) and `backend/tests/test_qdrant_isolation.py`. `tenant_filter(client_id: uuid.UUID) -> Filter` accepts only a real `uuid.UUID` instance — `isinstance(client_id, uuid.UUID)`, rejecting `None`, `""`, a plain `str`, an `int`, and even a UUID-shaped `str` — raising `TypeError` for anything else. Why: tenant identity already exists as a `uuid.UUID` by the time it reaches Qdrant (it comes from the verified token/database per the engineering rules), so accepting a looser type here would only hide an upstream bug; requiring the real type also forces the matched value to always be `uuid.UUID`'s own canonical lowercase `str()` form, so there is exactly one way a payload's `client_id` string can ever match. The function returns exactly one `must` condition (`FieldCondition(key=CLIENT_ID_FIELD, match=MatchValue(value=str(client_id)))`) and structurally cannot return `should`/`must_not` or an empty `Filter()` — an empty filter matches every point in Qdrant, which would be a silent cross-tenant leak.

  Hybrid outer-filter finding (run once, live, per the approved design; not asserted by any committed test): with `qdrant-client==1.19.1` against the pinned `qdrant/qdrant:v1.19.1` server, a `query_points()` hybrid call (two `Prefetch` entries plus `FusionQuery(fusion=Fusion.RRF)`) with `tenant_filter` applied **only** to the outer `query_filter` and to neither `Prefetch`, returned byte-for-byte the same result as applying it to both prefetches (and adding it to the outer query on top of both prefetches also changed nothing) — the outer filter alone did not leak in this run. This is **not** relied on: the committed tests assert only the mandated configuration (filter inside both prefetches), because relying on outer-only filtering is unverified beyond this one empirical check, is not documented as a guaranteed Qdrant contract, and a small per-`Prefetch` `limit` could still let another tenant's candidates crowd out a tenant's own genuine matches before fusion even runs (a correctness risk distinct from the leak question, observed while probing this — see the open marker below for 3.1). Re-verified at Task 1.3.e (H1 housekeeping): re-ran the same probe fresh this session — unfiltered dense control, unfiltered sparse control, filtered dense (A), filtered sparse (A), filtered hybrid (A) with the filter in both prefetches, and the same hybrid query with the filter ALSO added to the outer query on top of both prefetches — the outer-plus-both-prefetches variant again returned byte-for-byte identical ids, scores and ordering to the both-prefetches-only variant. a wrong or unknown secret behaves **exactly** like no secret at all — a fresh visitor is created and 200 is returned, so the endpoint can never be used to test whether a given secret is merely wrong versus never having existed; (6) a draft key from an allowed origin **succeeds**, with `test_mode` set in the response (docs/SPEC.md §6.3: draft keys work from allowed origins) — this is a success path, not a failure category; (7) the one true failure category — unknown key, missing or disallowed origin, a suspended key, and a non-active tenant — all produce one byte-identical response: a fixed 403 body, never `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, with `Vary: Origin` present on every response regardless of outcome, so none of the four conditions can be distinguished from any other (no oracle);   Key-selection order for decode: current key is tried first, then the previous key if one is configured and the current key's attempt fails, otherwise `InvalidSessionToken` is raised — exactly matching the task's own plain-English description. The unverified `kid` header is read (via `jwt.get_unverified_header()`, itself wrapped so a malformed header just means "no ordering hint," not a crash) and used **only** to swap that order — trying the previous key first specifically when `kid` unambiguously names it and not the current key — while both configured keys are *always* still tried regardless of what `kid` says, so a missing, wrong, or attacker-forged `kid` can never skip a real verification attempt, only reorder two attempts that both still happen. `decode_session_token()` raises one exception type, `InvalidSessionToken`, for every failure category (expired, forged, wrong `aud`/`iss`, a missing claim, wrong/no key, a tampered signature, a `kid` matching neither key, or a `tid`/`sub` that isn't a well-formed UUID) — deliberately no distinct subclass per cause, so nothing about *why* a token failed is ever visible to a caller from the exception type alone. `test_config_guard.py`'s `ALLOWED_JWT_KEY_CALLERS` (started empty at 1.4.a) gets its first real entry, `app/auth/tokens.py` — proved by hand with a scratch caller file under `backend/app/` (caught by the guard with the expected message, then removed, guard passing again, real files confirmed untouched).

  `get_current_visitor(request, session)`: (a) `Authorization` must be exactly `"Bearer <token>"` — a single space, non-empty token, no trailing text, case-sensitive `"Bearer"` — anything else (missing header, wrong scheme, empty token, extra text, no separating space) is a 401; (b) `decode_session_token()` (1.4.b) — any `InvalidSessionToken` is a 401, proving the WIRING with a hand-built expired token, a tampered signature, and a token signed with an unrelated key, rather than re-deriving all of 1.4.b's own 18 cryptographic tests; (c) the request's `Origin` (via `request.headers.getlist("origin")`, so a missing or repeated header also fails) must equal the token's own `org` claim EXACTLY — a **direct equality check**, deliberately NOT `origin_is_allowed()` (1.4.f): that function answers "is this origin on a site key's allow-list" (checked once, at session-creation time, 1.4.g); this question is narrower and different — "is this the exact origin THIS token was issued for" — checked on every subsequent authenticated request, and conflating the two would let a token minted for one allowed origin be replayed from a DIFFERENT origin that also happens to be on the same site key's allow-list, which the `org` claim binding exists specifically to prevent (docs/SPEC.md §4.3's own "Origin binding" rule); (d) tenant and site-key status via the 60-second TTL cache below — a non-`active` tenant or a `suspended` site key (draft and live both continue to work, matching 1.4.g's own session-creation rule) is a 401, checked against the cached value, never a fresh read on every request.

  **Why an extra lookup exists that the cache doesn't cover**: the JWT carries no `site_key_id` claim (1.4.b's claim set is fixed: `iss`/`aud`/`sub`/`tid`/`org`/`exp`/`kid`), so checking "site key status" requires first resolving the visitor's `site_key_id` via `vid` — one indexed, primary-key-scoped lookup on `visitors`, done on every request, NOT behind the 60-second cache. This is deliberate: a visitor's `site_key_id` is immutable once set (no code path anywhere changes it after `create_visitor`), so it can never go stale, unlike the two STATUSES, which really can change — that's what the cache exists for. A stricter reading of docs/SPEC.md §4.3's "no DB hit per request" would need this resolution cached too; noted as an UNCERTAIN marker below rather than silently over-building a second cache for an immutable mapping that costs one indexed lookup per request either way.

  **Cache design** (`StatusCache`, keyed by `(tenant_id, site_key_id)`): lives on `app.state.status_cache` (the same place `Settings` itself already lives, `app/main.py`'s `create_app()`), created lazily on first use — NOT a module-level `lru_cache` singleton like `get_settings()`/`get_engine()`. This means every `create_app()` call gets a fresh, empty cache automatically: no cross-test leakage is possible (a new FastAPI app has a new `app.state` namespace), and no `cache_clear()` step needed anywhere, unlike the existing singletons. Tests inject a controllable clock by pre-seeding `app.state.status_cache = StatusCache(clock=fake_clock)` before the first request. Keyed by `(tenant_id, site_key_id)` together, not `site_key_id` alone (which is already a globally-unique UUID) — matches this project's established tenant-scoping philosophy (never trust an id in isolation) and is what makes cross-tenant isolation trivially provable by construction of the key itself, proved directly in the tests by inspecting the cache's own stored entries, not just the HTTP outcome. **Cache-miss behavior**: a fresh DB read (one query each for `tenants.status` and `site_keys.status`, the latter also scoped by `tenant_id`) populates the cache with whatever it finds. **Deleted tenant/site-key**: `None` (row not found) is cached and treated as a plain, cacheable status value — it fails the "must be active/live" check the exact same way `"suspended"` does, and caching it too means a token for a permanently-deleted identity doesn't force a DB read on every single request either, matching the same "no DB hit per request" spirit as any other cached status.

- 2026-09-29: Step 1.5.a — pure `RateLimiter` (`backend/app/ratelimit.py`, new; `backend/tests/test_ratelimit.py`, new). Framework-agnostic: no imports from `fastapi`, `app.config`, or anything web-specific, matching `TenantScopedRepository`'s own layering precedent (`app/tenancy/repository.py`). Four decisions: (1) **sliding window log, not fixed window**: a fixed window lets a caller send up to 2x the limit in a burst straddling a window boundary (limit's worth just before, limit's worth just after — both buckets individually "under limit"), which is exactly the deliberate-abuse shape this exists to catch (docs/SPEC.md §9); a sliding window log (each key's own deque of recent request timestamps, pruned from the front as it goes) closes that gap directly. (2) **sliding-window-LOG chosen over token-bucket/leaky-bucket**: this project's own requirement is a flat "N per trailing window" count with no smoothing/burst-allowance requirement, so the log approach implements it with no extra tunables (bucket size, refill rate) to get wrong and no more code than the fixed-window version it replaces (rule 11) — no evidence a more elaborate algorithm is needed. (3) **limit/window fixed at construction, not per-check**: one `RateLimiter` instance is one policy; allowing different limits/windows per call for the *same* key would corrupt that key's own timestamp log's meaning (the log is only interpretable relative to one window). 1.5.c's `(IP, site_key)` policy and 1.5.e's broader per-IP policy are two different policies and will use two separate `RateLimiter` instances with disjoint key spaces, not one instance juggling two limits. (4) **rejected attempts are never recorded**: falls out of `check()`'s own ordering (the `len(attempts) >= limit` test happens strictly before the `append(now)` call) — no special-casing needed. Justification: a client that correctly backs off after a 429 must not have its next legitimate attempt further delayed by the rejected one; test (e) confirms this directly (a rejected attempt at t=2 does not push the recovery point past what the two genuine attempts at t=0/t=1 alone would require). (5) **memory bounding via full-sweep-per-check pruning**: `_prune_expired` sweeps every currently-tracked key on every single `check()` call (not just the key being checked), deleting any key whose deque empties out — pruning only the checked key would leak forever for a key that is checked exactly once and never rechecked, since nothing else would ever trigger its cleanup. Cost is O(number of currently-active keys) per check, judged acceptable at this project's realistic scale (one in-process limiter on a single API instance, docs/SPEC.md §9) — no LRU cap or background sweep thread built without evidence it's needed (rule 11). This sweep-every-key-on-every-check design is deliberate, not an oversight: it costs O(K) per `check()` call (K = currently-tracked distinct keys) regardless of which key is being checked, acceptable today (one endpoint, one API instance, small K) but flagged to reconsider before this limiter is reused for `/chat` in Step 4.1 — much higher call frequency (per message) and a larger K (all active visitors) would make that O(K)-per-check cost worth revisiting, e.g. via Redis (already docs/SPEC.md §17's named answer at scale). Injectable clock: `clock: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic`, same pattern as Task 1.4.h's `StatusCache`. Filename/class name kept as originally planned: `app/ratelimit.py` (matching the existing single-word module convention — `app/qdrant.py`, `app/db.py`, `app/health.py`, `app/worker.py`), class `RateLimiter`.

  Tests (all offline, `_FakeClock` injectable-clock pattern from `test_dependencies.py`, no real sleeps, no database, no network): (a) exactly `limit` requests allowed, the `limit+1`th rejected; (b) a blocked key becomes allowed again once the full window elapses via `clock.advance()`; (c) the sliding-vs-fixed-window proof — `limit=10, window=60`, a full burst of 10 requests concentrated at t=1059.0–1059.9 (all allowed), then one more at t=1060.1 correctly rejected (a naive fixed window bucketing on `floor(t/60)` would wrongly allow this, since 1060.1 falls in a fresh bucket with its own empty counter — a sliding window's trailing-60s check from 1060.1 still contains the full burst); (d) two independent keys never share a counter; (e) a rejected attempt is not counted and does not further delay recovery, confirmed by advancing the clock to exactly when the two genuine (non-rejected) attempts alone would age out, not later; (f) memory bounding — 50 one-off keys each checked once (`len(limiter._attempts) == 50`), then the clock advances well past the window and one unrelated new key is checked, confirming all 50 stale entries are swept away in that single call (`len(limiter._attempts) == 1`, only the new key remains) — proving the full-sweep behavior, not just inspection.

No ASSUMPTION/UNCERTAIN markers needed — every design choice (sliding vs. fixed window, log vs. token/leaky bucket, construction-time vs. per-check limit/window, rejected-attempt semantics, the memory-bounding sweep) was fully specified by the task itself or resolved directly with justification recorded above; no open questions remain for 1.5.a's own scope. Per-IP first because it is the broader, cheaper-to-reject check, and must trip even when no site-key-specific state exists yet (docs/SPEC.md §16's "many new visitors from one IP hit the IP cap") — proved directly by `test_per_ip_limiter_checked_first_and_can_trip_before_any_site_key_state_exists` and `test_per_ip_limiter_trips_across_many_different_site_keys`.

The `(IP, site_key)` limiter's key is `f"{len(ip)}:{ip}:{site_key}"` (`_site_key_rate_limit_key()`), a netstring-style length-prefix encoding, not naive concatenation: `site_key` is fully client-controlled (`SessionRequest.site_key` has no charset/length constraint) and read from the request body BEFORE any DB validation, so a plain `f"{ip}:{site_key}"` would let a crafted `site_key` value collide two different `(ip, site_key)` pairs onto the same combined string (e.g. `ip="1.2.3.4"`, `site_key="5:x"` vs. `ip="1.2.3.4:5"`, `site_key="x"`), letting one visitor's requests silently share, or poison, another's rate-limit counter — a real concern given this is a [SECURITY] task. Length-prefixing the IP makes the encoding provably injective regardless of what characters either part contains.

Five decisions confirmed:

  (a) **Table scope and field types**: 2.1 owns exactly `sources`, `documents`, `db_connections`, `jobs` — **`verified_domains` and `audit_log` are explicitly deferred to Step 2.2** (Domain verification `[SECURITY]`), not built now, even though §5.2 lists them in the same Postgres bullet: 2.2 is independently security-reviewed and the tables are meaningless without their own verification/audit logic, so building them ahead of that review would leave an unreviewed, unused `[SECURITY]`-adjacent surface sitting in the schema. `sources.config`: JSONB, matching `plans.limits`'s own precedent (1.2's decision (5) — most concrete fields are adapter-specific and not yet needed as structured columns). `jobs`: UUID PK (consistent with every other table so far) and **`source_id` nullable, a deliberate decision, not an afterthought** — reconcile and refresh-scheduling jobs are not always tied to one source row. `db_connections`' credential fields: **structured columns, not JSONB** — see the dedicated research below.

  **`db_connections` credential-column research** (done before building 2.1.a, as instructed): does `Settings`' `SecretStr` + guarded-accessor pattern (`qdrant_api_key_str()`, etc.) translate directly to a SQLAlchemy ORM column? **No — confirmed by reading the code, not assumed**: `SecretStr` is a pydantic `BaseModel` feature — pydantic's own `BaseModel.__repr__`/`__str__` dumps every field by default, which is exactly the failure mode `SecretStr` exists to mask. `backend/app/db.py`'s `Base(DeclarativeBase)` has **no custom `__repr__`** anywhere in this codebase (confirmed by grep) — SQLAlchemy's own declarative default `__repr__` is the plain `<ClassName object at 0x...>`, which does **not** dump column values. So the specific leak vector `SecretStr` defends against doesn't exist the same way for a plain ORM column with no custom `__repr__` — a `SecretStr`-equivalent *column type* would be solving a problem this layer doesn't actually have.

  The real risk surface for a DB-stored credential is different, and the proposed smallest correct equivalent addresses that surface instead, one layer down (repository/model, not Settings): (1) **encryption at rest**, spec-mandated explicitly (§5.6: "Credentials are encrypted at rest") — the actual primary defense, not an application-level nicety; mechanism (pgcrypto vs. application-level encryption, e.g. `cryptography`'s Fernet with a key sourced from a new required `Settings` field, matching every other secret's existing discipline) is **not decided here** — both are well-known/standard (rule 11), compared live at 2.1.a's own build time, not assumed from this planning session (matching 1.3.b's own "re-verify at build time" precedent for exactly this kind of choice); (2) a **guarded accessor method** on whichever repository owns `db_connections` access (e.g. a `get_decrypted_credentials()`-shaped method), mirroring `qdrant_api_key_str()`'s "one explicit call that unwraps the secret, never log this" pattern — never raw column access anywhere else; (3) a **new guard test**, the same AST-based allow-list mechanism `test_config_guard.py` already uses for `database_url_str()`/`qdrant_api_key_str()`/`jwt_signing_key_str()`, scoped to this new accessor instead — either extending that existing file or a small new sibling test, decided at 2.1.a's own build time; (4) **never include these columns in a raw dict/model dump**, matching `_public_widget_config()`'s own explicit-field-allow-list precedent (`app/auth/routes.py`) — relevant once an admin endpoint exists to list `db_connections` (Phase 6), noted here as a forward pointer, not built now.

  (b) **Job claiming mechanism**: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` with the `pending → running` status flip in the same transaction — a well-known, standard Postgres queue pattern (rule 11), not a custom scheme. Confirmed necessary now, not merely future-proofing: docs/SPEC.md §17's own scale-out trigger table says "Queue lag above 5 minutes → Add worker instances (**same image**)" — multiple concurrent workers are an anticipated, spec-named event, so the claiming query must already be safe against double-claiming even though only one `worker` Compose service exists today.

  (c) **2.1 builds the real job-processing loop** (claim → dispatch-by-`job_type` → mark done/failed/retry), proven with a no-op/stub handler — not schema-and-enqueue-only. No real crawl/upload/database-sync logic is built here (that stays 2.4–2.8's job, per §18's own step split); the loop mechanism itself is what "job queue" in this step's own title means, matching `ensure_collection()`'s own precedent (1.3.c) of a real, fully-tested function built ahead of its eventual real caller.

  (d) **`ensure_collection()` wiring bundled into Step 2.1** as its own subtask (2.1.g), now that Phase 2 — specifically this step — is where it first becomes relevant (reassigned from Step 1.3.c's own marker at the Step 1.6 close-out, 2026-09-30).

  (e) **Confirmed, no action**: the `client_id`-canonical-lowercase-form marker and the `CLIENT_ACCESS_ALLOWLIST` marker (both recorded at 1.3.d/1.3.e) stay correctly owned by Step 2.5 (Embedding and Qdrant upserts) — 2.1 has no relationship to either, since nothing in 2.1's own scope ever calls Qdrant.

  **[SECURITY] A real, live leak found and fixed while writing the C1 coverage, not a pre-existing test gap being closed**: proving C1 required a genuine `IngestRepository` failure path, so a wrong/rotated `db_connection_encryption_key` decrypt attempt was reproduced live against the real test database. `str(exc)` on the resulting `sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError` contained the literal key value, verbatim — SQLAlchemy's default `StatementError.__str__()` embeds every bound parameter of the failing statement (here, the key itself), and `app/db.py`'s `create_async_engine()` call does not set `hide_parameters=True`. This directly contradicted `get_decrypted_credentials()`'s own "never log this" comment: if this exception is ever logged (normal handling for an unhandled exception), the key ends up in logs. Flagged to the user before writing C1 as originally worded (asserting the key's absence), since that test would otherwise have failed, inverting its own purpose, and fixing the underlying leak was beyond this task's stated "behaviour must stay identical" scope without confirmation. User confirmed (2026-09-30): fix at the source (catch-and-re-raise-sanitized), not `hide_parameters=True` at any scope — an engine-wide setting would strip bound parameters from every exception across the whole app, including ordinary non-sensitive queries where seeing real parameter values is genuinely useful for debugging, too broad a trade for one credential-specific leak; a query-scoped `hide_parameters` was judged a blunter, less certain mechanism than handling it at the source.

  **Fix**: `backend/app/ingest/repository.py` gained a new `CredentialEncryptionError` exception class (module-level, following `app/auth/tokens.py`'s `InvalidSessionToken` convention — a fixed, generic message, documented as never containing the original exception's string form). Both `create_db_connection()` and `get_decrypted_credentials()` now catch `SQLAlchemyError` from their own `pgp_sym_encrypt`/`pgp_sym_decrypt` statement and re-raise `CredentialEncryptionError`, always **outside** the `except` block — confirmed live, before choosing this, that `raise ... from None` alone does **not** clear `__context__` (only `__suppress_context__`, which affects default traceback printing, not programmatic access), so a chain-walking check like this project's own `assert_secret_not_in_exception_chain` would still have found the leaked key via `__context__` even with `from None`. Raising after leaving the `except` block entirely (matching `decode_session_token()`'s own established, commented convention for the identical reason) avoids Python setting `__context__` at all. `create_db_connection()`'s encrypt statement received the identical treatment even though a well-formed, length-validated key cannot itself fail *encryption* (only decryption has a "wrong key" failure mode) — the leak mechanism is that the key is a bound parameter of that statement too, so any other exception during that same `execute()` call (a dropped connection, a timeout) would carry it the same way. No live test was written for the encrypt path specifically: unlike decrypt's clean, realistic "wrong key" trigger, there is no realistic way to force `pgp_sym_encrypt()` itself to fail with a well-formed key without an artificial, unrelated fault (e.g. severing the connection mid-statement), and this project's live-only testing discipline argues against fabricating one.

  **`enqueue()` vs. `claim_next_job()`/`mark_job_succeeded()`/`mark_job_failed()` placement, applying `create_tenant()`'s own precedent (app/tenancy/repository.py) in both directions**: `enqueue()` is an `IngestRepository` method — enqueueing always happens on behalf of an already-known tenant's own action (a source being added, a scheduled refresh), so a real `tenant_id` is always already available, the same reasoning `create_visitor()`/`create_conversation()` already rely on. The other three are standalone functions in a new sibling module, `queue.py`, not `IngestRepository` methods: the worker claims and marks jobs across every tenant, with no tenant identity at all at call time, so they structurally cannot fit `IngestRepository`'s own invariant (construction always requires a real `tenant_id`) — the exact inverse of why `create_tenant()`/`get_site_key_by_key()` are standalone (no tenant identity *yet*, there; no tenant identity *ever*, here).

  **Claiming mechanism, verified live, not assumed**: a single `UPDATE jobs SET status='running', updated_at=now() WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status='pending' AND next_run_at <= now() ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING *` — the standard, well-known Postgres queue idiom (rule 11), constructed in SQLAlchemy as an ORM-enabled `update(Job).where(Job.id == select(Job.id)...with_for_update(skip_locked=True).limit(1).scalar_subquery()).values(...).returning(Job)`, executed via `session.execute(stmt).scalar_one_or_none()`. Chosen over a separate `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` followed by a second `UPDATE` statement: one statement is inherently "read the next row and flip it in the same transaction," with no window between the two for a second concurrent caller to see the same row as still pending. Compiled SQL rendered and inspected by hand first (confirming `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lands after `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1`, Postgres's required clause order), then executed live against the real test database and confirmed to return a genuine, correctly-flipped `Job` ORM instance with a real read-back. `claim_next_job()` does not commit internally — matching every other repository/service function in this codebase (only `app/auth/routes.py`'s own endpoint-level code calls `session.commit()`); the caller (2.1.d's worker loop, or a test) owns the transaction boundary. This does not weaken the concurrency guarantee: Postgres holds a `FOR UPDATE` row lock from the moment the statement executes, not from commit, so concurrent callers are already correctly serialized before anyone commits — and a caller that crashes before committing simply rolls back, automatically restoring the job to "pending" for the next claimer, an unplanned but useful self-healing property of a real transaction over a hand-rolled `claimed_by` column.

  **The concurrency proof itself (the one that actually matters, per this task's own framing)**: `test_queue.py::test_claim_next_job_concurrency_proof` seeds 10 real pending jobs, then runs 13 concurrent `claim_next_job()` calls via `asyncio.gather()`, each on its own `db_session()` (a genuinely separate connection/transaction, not a sequential loop simulating concurrency) — asserts all 10 jobs were claimed, each exactly once (no double-claim, no silent skip), and the 3 oversubscribed callers cleanly received `None`. Re-run 8 times standalone before being folded into the suite; stable every time. A hand-written, throwaway version of the same proof (15 concurrent callers against 14 genuinely pending rows, due to leftover state from earlier manual verification) was run first, live, before writing the permanent test — 14 unique claims, 1 clean `None`, 0 double-claims, matching this task's own "prove it live, not just in the permanent test" discipline.

  **Backoff formula and its defaults**: `next_run_at = clock() + timedelta(seconds=base_seconds * 2**attempts)`, `attempts` counted *after* incrementing for the current failure, using an injectable clock (`clock: Callable[[], datetime] = lambda: datetime.now(UTC)`, matching `RateLimiter`'s own `clock: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic` pattern, `app/ratelimit.py`) so a test can assert the exact resulting timestamp. `job_retry_base_seconds` defaults to 60 and `job_max_attempts` (see below) defaults to 5 — together giving retries at 2/4/8/16 minutes before the job becomes permanently `failed`, a reasonable schedule for a background ingestion job (crawl/upload/database-sync/reconcile): nothing user-facing or latency-sensitive is waiting on it, unlike docs/SPEC.md §14's email-retry precedent (5 attempts, ~1 min to 12 h) which this deliberately does not copy verbatim — email's own schedule spans hours because a human eventually reads the result; a job's own worker loop just needs to not hammer a transient failure.

The column's DB-level `server_default=5` stays in place, now purely as an inert defensive floor for any insert that bypasses `enqueue()`, no longer the actual source of truth for the sanctioned path. Flagged to the user before building, per rule 11 ("if anything looks wrong, say so first") — confirmed as the right reconciliation, not a real conflict.

Connection refused` in about 1.3s (fast, not a hang; confirmed the message contains only host/port, no credentials). Before this task, `run()` never touched the database at all, so this test never depended on one being reachable; this task's own loop would have made it crash on its first iteration, before ever receiving the test's SIGTERM, turning a previously-DB-independent, always-passing test into a flaky/broken one. Fixed by design, not by changing the test: the per-iteration claim/process step is wrapped in a broad `try/except Exception`, logging only the exception's *type* (never `str(exc)` — unlike 2.1.a/b's own pgcrypto statement-level leak, a connection-level failure's message has not been proven safe, so this stays defensively conservative rather than assuming it is), then treated exactly like "nothing was ready": sleep the poll interval, try again. The sleep itself is `asyncio.wait_for(stop.wait(), timeout=worker_poll_interval_seconds)`, not a plain `asyncio.sleep()`: it wakes immediately on `stop` being set (preserving SIGTERM responsiveness during an idle poll, not regressing 1.1.f's own instant-shutdown guarantee) while still bounding the wait to the configured interval. - 2026-10-01: Step 2.1.e — worker graceful shutdown. `backend/app/worker.py` (extended — a `"sleep"` test handler, the `app.tenancy`/`app.plans` model-import fix below, a per-claim log line, an explanatory comment on the loop itself); `backend/tests/test_worker.py` (extended — the real SIGTERM-mid-handler proof). `docker info` confirmed running first.

  **Design questions, answered before building, per the task's own request**: (1) option (a) confirmed — let the current job's handler finish, then exit without claiming another; pushing back was considered but there is no problem with it (handlers in 2.4-2.8 could be long-running, and a forced mid-write kill is a worse outcome than letting a crawl/upload finish). (2) confirmed out of scope: a job stuck in `"running"` forever because its own worker crashed hard (SIGKILL/OOM, no chance for graceful shutdown to run at all) is a separate problem needing a stuck-job reaper/lease-timeout mechanism, not anything a clean-SIGTERM handler can address — recorded as a new Open marker (see below), not built here.

  **The actual finding: no functional change was needed in `run()`'s own loop.** `while not stop.is_set():` (2.1.d) is already re-evaluated fresh at the top of every iteration, and `stop.set()` (the SIGTERM callback `main()` registers via `loop.add_signal_handler`) is a plain cooperative flag — it never cancels an in-flight `await _claim_and_process_one_job()`. So a signal arriving while a handler is actively running is only ever observed at the next iteration boundary, after that job has already run to completion and been marked succeeded/failed — exactly "finish what you started, claim nothing new," already true before this task touched a single line of loop logic. This was **confirmed live, not assumed**: a real `python -m app.worker` subprocess, a job whose handler sleeps, a real SIGTERM sent while the DB row's own status is polled to confirm `"running"`, repeated cleanly multiple times. The task's own two "design questions to resolve first" turned out to already be correctly answered by 2.1.d's own existing structure; the real work this task did was proving that rigorously and documenting the invariant explicitly in the code (a comment on the loop itself) so a future reader doesn't have to rediscover it by reasoning from scratch.

Needed because no *existing* handler could ever give the proof above a window to exercise — `noop` returns before the event loop gets a chance to do anything else. A second, explicitly-named registry entry (rather than overloading `_noop_handler` with a hidden sleep parameter) was chosen so a reader encountering `job_type="sleep"` understands its purpose (a controllable-delay utility) without needing to already know `noop` secretly supports a payload key — the job-queue literature's own common "debug sleep job" pattern for exactly this kind of worker-behavior testing.

- 2026-10-01: Step 2.1.f — worker healthcheck. `backend/app/worker.py` (extended — `HEARTBEAT_PATH`, `HEARTBEAT_STALE_MULTIPLIER`, `_write_heartbeat()`, `check_heartbeat_fresh()`, wired into `run()`'s own loop); `deploy/docker-compose.yml` (worker service gains a real `healthcheck:`, resolves the Step-2.1-owned marker); `backend/tests/test_worker.py` (3 new tests). `docker info` confirmed running first.

  **Mechanism**: a file-based heartbeat, since the worker has no HTTP server (unlike the api service's own `/ready`, Task 1.4.j). `HEARTBEAT_PATH = Path("/tmp/worker-heartbeat")` — not an arbitrary choice: the container runs `read_only: true` with a tmpfs `/tmp` (`x-app-hardening`, applied to worker too), so `/tmp` is close to the only writable location available. The file's own content is the write time itself (`time.time()`, plain text), not reliance on the filesystem's mtime — a human or script can `cat` it and understand it immediately, and it sidesteps any mtime-semantics subtlety across tmpfs/`exec`-into-container edge cases. `run()`'s loop calls `_write_heartbeat(HEARTBEAT_PATH)` as the very first statement inside its existing per-iteration `try:` block — before the claim attempt, every iteration, including an idle one with nothing to claim: an "only on a claimed job" heartbeat could not distinguish idle-but-alive from wedged, since a worker with no pending jobs for a while would look identical to one that stopped iterating entirely. A write failure is caught by the same existing exception handler as a claim/mark failure (no second try/except): a worker that cannot write its own heartbeat is arguably unhealthy in a real sense too, not just logging-wise. `HEARTBEAT_PATH` is referenced by its global name at the call site, not left to `_write_heartbeat()`'s own default parameter — confirmed live that a default argument's value is bound once, at function-definition time, so monkeypatching the module attribute alone would not otherwise reach a call relying on the default.

  **Freshness threshold**: `HEARTBEAT_STALE_MULTIPLIER = 3`, multiplied by `worker_poll_interval_seconds` at check time (6s with the 2s default) — a multiple of that setting, not a fixed number of seconds, since the heartbeat is written once per iteration and an idle iteration's own wait is already bounded by that same value. 3x covers one full normal idle-wait between writes plus headroom for an occasional slow iteration (a DB round-trip hiccup, a GC pause), comfortably under `x-healthcheck-timing`'s own `retries*interval=25s` detection floor — this threshold, not Docker's own probe schedule, is what actually decides "stale". `check_heartbeat_fresh()` is the one function both the real Docker healthcheck (`deploy/docker-compose.yml`'s own `python3 -c "..."` one-liner, matching the api service's own no-curl-in-the-image convention) and this file's own tests call — not duplicated shell-script and Python freshness logic that could silently drift apart.

  **ASSUMPTION, recorded in `worker.py` itself**: a genuinely long-running handler (2.4-2.8) that runs longer than `HEARTBEAT_STALE_MULTIPLIER * worker_poll_interval_seconds` would make the heartbeat go stale while the worker is still healthy, just busy — the heartbeat is written once per iteration *start*, not progressively during a handler's own execution. Not a problem today: every registered handler (`noop`, `sleep`, both test/proof-only) is instant or a short, test-controlled duration. Revisit once a genuinely long-running handler exists: either it must report its own progress by writing the heartbeat periodically during its own work, or this threshold must grow to cover the longest expected single-job duration.

  **Live Compose proof**: `make up` (after a transient, unrelated first-attempt build failure — a pip `--require-hashes` hash-verification error on retry-cached layers, gone on a clean rebuild, not reproducible, not related to this task's own changes) — worker reached `(healthy)` within 11 seconds of container start. Wedge simulated via `docker kill --signal=SIGSTOP widgetplatform-worker-1` (freezes the worker's own PID 1 without touching the container or its separate healthcheck-probe processes, which run as distinct `docker exec` invocations in the same PID namespace and are unaffected by a SIGSTOP targeted at PID 1 alone) — confirmed the heartbeat file genuinely stopped advancing (unchanged across a 4-second poll) before watching: polled `docker compose ps` every 3s, observed the transition from `(healthy)` to `(unhealthy)` at the ~12-second mark into the poll loop (consistent with the ~6s staleness threshold plus Docker's own 5-consecutive-failing-probes requirement). `docker kill --signal=SIGCONT` resumed the process; recovered to `(healthy)` within one probe cycle (~3s) — Docker only requires a single successful probe to flip back healthy, unlike the 5 consecutive failures needed to flip unhealthy, a standard, expected asymmetry, not something this task needed to build. A genuine, unrelated finding surfaced mid-proof: the worker logged a real `ProgrammingError` every idle iteration because `make up` does not run migrations (`migrate` is `profiles: ["tools"]`, run explicitly) — the fresh `postgres` volume had no `jobs` table yet. Confirmed this is exactly what it looked like (not a regression): running `docker compose run --rm migrate` made the errors stop immediately, and the worker was correctly reported `(healthy)` throughout, even while every claim attempt failed — proving the heartbeat's own intended property live, not just in a test: liveness and job-processing success are genuinely different things, and this mechanism only ever claims the former. `make down`: clean, `docker ps -a` confirms no leftover containers.

No UNCERTAIN markers: every design question in this task's own scope was resolved with recorded reasoning. No new TODO: the Step-2.1-owned worker-healthcheck marker is resolved and removed from Open markers below, not left open.

  Root cause, confirmed live before building anything: `python:3.12.14-slim-trixie`'s own last build has not yet picked up these `trixie-security` patches. Force-pulled the exact pinned tag — Docker reported a newer manifest, but `dpkg -l` inside the freshly-pulled image still showed the same vulnerable `...u2` versions, so this is not a stale-local-cache issue; the upstream image tag itself hasn't been rebuilt against the patched packages yet. Separately confirmed, via `apt-get update && apt-cache policy` run live inside the base image, that the patched `...u3` versions ARE already published and resolvable from Debian's own `deb.debian.org/debian-security trixie-security/main` repo — the fix exists upstream, just not yet baked into this image tag.

  **Fix applied**: `backend/Dockerfile`'s final stage gained one new `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends --only-upgrade <pkg>=<exact ...u3 version> ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` step, placed after the existing pip-uninstall/ensurepip-removal step and before `WORKDIR /app` (OS-level hardening grouped together, before any application code is copied in, standard layer-ordering practice). Pinned to the exact patched version for each of the five packages (`openssl`, `libssl3t64`, `openssl-provider-legacy`, `libpcre2-8-0`), not a bare `--only-upgrade` with no version and not a blanket `apt-get upgrade` (which would pull in an unbounded, unreviewed set of changes) — this fails loudly at build time if a pinned version ever disappears from the repo, rather than silently installing whatever happens to be newest. Apt lists cleaned up in the same `RUN` layer, the standard Debian/Docker convention (this Dockerfile had no prior `apt-get` usage to match an existing convention against; this establishes the first one).

  Verified: rebuilt the image fresh, re-ran the identical grype invocation — all 5 High findings gone; only Medium/Low/Negligible Python-stdlib CVEs remain (the same ones already present before this fix, unrelated, below the `--fail-on high` threshold). `dpkg -l` inside the new image confirms all four package names now report `...u3`. `sh deploy/smoke-image.sh widgetplatform-backend:scan`: all 8 checks pass, unaffected. `make lint` clean. Full `backend/tests` without a test database: **329 passed, 126 skipped** (unchanged — no Python/test code touched). Image size: **89.59 MB → 93.19 MB** (+3.6 MB), confirmed via a side-by-side rebuild of the pre-patch Dockerfile under a throw-away tag, compared, then deleted — small and expected, these are point-patches, not major version bumps. `git status --short`: exactly `backend/Dockerfile` and `PROJECT_SPEC.md`, `.env` correctly absent.

  **Who calls it, and why (confirmed, not just proposed)**: `migrate` (the existing Compose deploy step), not the worker's own startup path. `migrate` already is exactly the "run idempotent setup steps once before the stack comes up" service (it already runs `alembic upgrade head` this way); `ensure_collection()` (1.3.c) is the same kind of one-shot idempotent setup step, just for Qdrant instead of Postgres.   **Mechanism**: `backend/entrypoint.sh`'s existing `migrate` case gains a second step: `alembic upgrade head` (no longer `exec`'d — only the final command in the script should be, so it becomes PID 1) followed by `exec python -m app.qdrant`. `set -eu` (already present) means a failed migration aborts the script with Alembic's own exit code before `app.qdrant` ever runs. `app/qdrant.py` gains a `main()` / `if __name__ == "__main__":` CLI entrypoint (`asyncio.run()` over a small `_ensure_collection_and_close()` coroutine: `get_qdrant_client()` → `ensure_collection()` → `client.close()`), mirroring `app/worker.py`'s own `main()` error-handling style exactly — a clean one-line message to stderr and `sys.exit(1)` on `SettingsError` or `CollectionSchemaMismatch`, never a traceback (both exceptions' own messages are already proven free of secrets, confirmed by re-reading their docstrings before relying on that). A superuser bypasses every permission check, by definition — `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON audit_log FROM widgetplatform` was proven live to execute cleanly and have **zero effect**: a probe table created, revoked-from, then successfully `UPDATE`d and `DELETE`d anyway by the same role, then reconfirmed on `audit_log` itself once the real migration existed. The statement is still written into 2.2.b's migration (harmless, and it becomes real enforcement automatically, with zero further migration work, the instant the role split below lands) — but **today, 2.2.h's AST-based guard is the ONLY real enforcement against `UPDATE`/`DELETE` on `audit_log`, not a secondary layer under a working primary one.** `backend/tests/test_alembic.py::test_audit_log_update_delete_currently_succeeds_because_widgetplatform_is_a_superuser` is the permanent, automated proof of this exact, current, honest state — it is expected to start *failing* the moment the role split lands, at which point it must be rewritten to assert the opposite, not deleted.

Building an unguarded fetch now and retrofitting 2.3's protection later would leave a real, exploitable hole in between, which rule 11 ("security requirements... always win over simplicity") forecloses. **Resolution: ship DNS-only verification now** (a DNS TXT lookup to a resolver carries no equivalent outbound-fetch-to-attacker-content risk), using the spec's own "file, meta tag, **or** DNS" wording to sequence safely; file/meta-tag verification is deferred until immediately after Step 2.3 lands, so it can reuse that step's real SSRF guard from day one rather than 2.2 building a scoped-down duplicate of logic 2.3 will also need (rule 4). `dnspython` is approved as a new runtime dependency under rule 8 — name, purpose (TXT-record lookup; Python's stdlib has no TXT-query capability at all, confirmed by reading `socket`'s own API) and no viable alternative considered (shelling out to `dig`/`host` would trade a vetted, hash-pinned Python dependency for a fragile, un-pinned system-binary dependency) — its exact current version is to be re-verified live against PyPI at 2.2.d's own build time, not assumed from this planning session, matching every prior dependency addition's own precedent (1.3.b, 1.4.b, 2.1.a). `httpx`'s promotion from a dev-only to a direct runtime dependency is deferred alongside file/meta-tag verification, for the same reason — nothing in 2.2's own DNS-only scope needs it. The verification token is generated fresh per claim attempt, tenant-and-attempt-specific, and is never reused across attempts or tenants — closing the "tenant B reuses tenant A's stale proof" gap flagged during this breakdown's own research.

  **Partial-unique-index approach, and why**: the global-uniqueness rule (Step 2.2 breakdown, decision (e)) needs a domain claimable again once revoked, which a plain, unconditional unique constraint can never allow without deleting the old row first — and deleting it would destroy the very audit trail `audit_log`/the revocation flow exists to keep. `Index("ix_verified_domains_domain_active_unique", "domain", unique=True, postgresql_where=text("status != 'revoked'"))` — confirmed live, by hand, before building (not assumed from memory): SQLAlchemy's `Index` genuinely supports a `postgresql_where` dialect kwarg, and it round-trips back off the `Index` object via `index.dialect_options["postgresql"]["where"]`, which is what the new test inspects directly. Deliberately on `domain` alone, never `(tenant_id, domain)` — the uniqueness is global, across every tenant, not a per-tenant scope.

  **`audit_log` has no `tenant_id` column — confirmed, not merely absent by oversight**: an audit entry records an ADMIN's own action, not a tenant's own action within its own scope — the exact thing `TenantScopedRepository` exists to enforce does not apply here, since no tenant is "operating" when a platform admin revokes a domain. docs/SPEC.md §15 independently confirms this by naming future `audit_log` actions (threshold overrides, plan changes) that don't belong to any single tenant either. `target_id` (nullable, no FK — `target_type` varies per action, so one FK could never fit every case) still names which row an action affected, without the table itself being tenant-scoped.

  **The database-level `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE` is explicitly flagged as NOT built here, and cannot be**: it is a privilege grant, not a schema object — SQLAlchemy's declarative mapping has no way to express it, and attempting to fake it at the ORM level (e.g. overriding `__setattr__` or omitting update/delete helper methods) would be exactly the kind of "looks enforced but isn't" surface this project's own discipline avoids elsewhere. A comment on `AuditLog` itself says so explicitly, naming 2.2.b as the task that must apply it, so nobody mistakes this model alone as the enforcement mechanism in the meantime.
